extracted.intended_audience: environmental advocates, public health professionals, affected consumers, journalists, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: A press-release–style advocacy summary about a legal challenge and rulemaking relating to requiring disclosure of so-called inert ingredients in pesticide products. Focus is on the regulatory status, public-health rationale, and proposed disclosure options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to disclose inert ingredients
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking that would require pesticides manufacturers to disclose the inert ingredients found in their products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earthjustice represents groups challenging the EPA for failing to complete such rulemaking; currently manufacturers are only required to list 'active' ingredients. Disclosure is presented as necessary because many inerts are hazardous or suspected toxic chemicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'inert' ingredient
rubrics_metrics.description: An inert ingredient is any ingredient that is 'not active,' or not targeted to killing a pest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although termed 'inert,' these chemicals can be hazardous and are often more toxic than active ingredients; the term may mislead consumers into believing such ingredients are harmless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling must identify ingredient identity (not just weight percent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Current pesticide labels only identify the weight percentage of inert ingredients, which often comprise 50 to 99 percent of a formulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listing only percentages misleads the public into thinking inerts are safe; advocates argue labels should identify the actual chemicals so consumers and medical professionals know what exposures exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of disclosure — two proposed alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's advanced notice of proposed rulemaking solicited comment on two alternatives: (1) require listing of all ingredients already identified as hazardous, or (2) require listing of all ingredients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comment period closed in April 2010; the press release frames these alternatives as the central policy choices the EPA must act on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-health justification for disclosure (clinical treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: When pesticide producers refuse to identify all the ingredients in pesticides, doctors are compromised in their ability to treat patients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate access to information on inert substances can make a critical difference in patient outcome; medical support was cited among public comments favoring disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer right-to-know and market-incentive rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers and users of pesticide products have a right to know all the ingredients so they can make more informed choices in the marketplace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public disclosure may lead to less exposure because consumers will likely choose informed-by-label products, and pesticide producers will likely respond by producing products with less hazardous inert ingredients.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA procedural obligation and timeline (petition/response rulemaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2006 coalition petition and subsequent litigation (2009) sought to compel EPA to begin rulemaking; EPA issued an ANPR and solicited comments but has taken no further action since the 2010 comment period closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a failure of administrative follow-through that justifies legal challenge to compel the agency to complete the rulemaking process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of prevalence and hazard of inerts
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA has identified hundreds of 'inert' chemicals as hazardous or potentially hazardous, and inerts often make up the majority of a product formulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Billions of pounds of pesticides enter food, homes, schools, public lands and waterways; the scale and documented hazard of inerts are used to support urgency for disclosure rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory baseline under FIFRA
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), pesticide manufacturers are required to list 'active' ingredients but are not required to disclose inert ingredients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory baseline explains why rulemaking is necessary to change labeling/disclosure obligations for inert ingredients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer misperception about 'inert' terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's 1997 studies found that many consumers have a misleading impression of the term 'inert ingredient,' believing it to indicate water or other harmless ingredients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports the argument that current labeling language is deceptive and that clearer disclosure is needed to protect consumers.
